document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting women of reproductive age and can cause infertility and pelvic pain. Its effects on fertility involve multiple processes that may also influence Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART). Peritoneal, deep infiltrating and ovarian disease may affect ovarian reserve, stimulation response, access for oocyte retrieval, procedural safety and endometrial receptivity. The place of surgery for ovarian endometriosis and endometriomas remains uncertain. This guideline examines how pelvic endometriosis and endometriomas affect ART outcomes and addresses management before and during ART, including intra-uterine insemination, with the aim of improving assisted-conception outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Endometriosis involves endometrium-like tissue outside the uterus and is estimated to affect 10% of women of reproductive age. It can have substantial physical, sexual, psychological and social consequences; symptoms vary, and some patients are asymptomatic. An estimated up to 50% of women presenting with infertility have endometriosis. Estimated monthly fecundability is 2–10% in women with endometriosis versus 20% in reproductive-age women without known fertility problems. Potential contributors to infertility include mechanical, inflammatory, hormonal, genetic and environmental factors. Pelvic adhesions and tubal obstruction can alter anatomy. Ovarian endometriomas occur in almost 50% of cases and are thought to injure ovarian tissue; histological studies describe cortical invasion, fibrosis and abnormal vascular networks. Compared with healthy ovaries and other benign ovarian cysts, endometriomas are associated with lower ovarian reserve, serum anti-Mullerian Hormone (AMH) and ultrasound antral follicle counts. A report found up to 38% reduction in AMH after ovarian cystectomy. Reserve loss associated with surgery is greater with bilateral disease and repeat surgery for recurrence; possible sources of injury include removal of healthy tissue during stripping, impaired blood supply, heat injury and local inflammation. Advanced maternal age, tubal obstruction or unsuccessful expectant management may necessitate in-vitro fertilization (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). Evidence on ART pregnancy outcomes is inconsistent and comes from comparisons with women without endometriosis or with other infertility causes. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses associated moderate or severe disease with fewer retrieved oocytes, poorer implantation and lower live birth rates. An analysis of 347,185 fresh and frozen ART cycles in The Society of Assisted Reproductive Technologies (SART) database found live birth rates similar to those for other infertility causes unless additional infertility factors were present. A retrospective study spanning 16years and 27,294 ART cycles suggested fewer oocytes with endometriosis but no effect on pregnancy or live birth rates. A review of 8 studies found fewer mature oocytes with endometrioma, while total embryos, high-quality embryos, implantation, clinical pregnancy and live birth rates were similar to controls. This BFS Policy and Practice guideline evaluates endometriosis-associated infertility and evidence-based management before and during ART, including IUI, to improve assisted-conception outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Materials and methods
document_sections.content: MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL were searched from inception through March 2022 for studies relevant to endometriosis management during ART. Search terms combined endometriosis or endometrioma with assisted reproductive techniques (ART), invitro fertilization (IVF), intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) and intrauterine insemination (IUI). Two authors, KS and MH, also screened references manually. Only English-language papers were included. All authors approved the topics, and identified studies were grouped by topic. Eligible studies diagnosed endometriosis through laparoscopy or non-invasive imaging. The guideline uses the 1996 revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine (rASRM) classification, which considers implant location and size and surgical adhesion severity: minimal (stage I), mild (II), moderate (III) and severe (stage IV). The guideline development group (GDG) applied GRADE, assigning ‘strong’ or ‘weak’ recommendations; where evidence was limited, expert-based advice was labelled ‘good practice points’. The guideline also makes research recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Governance
document_sections.content: The society ratified the guideline following consultation with the BFS Executive Committee and Membership under its agreed protocol.

document_sections.heading: Hormonal therapies as an adjuvant/pre-treatment to IVF
document_sections.content: A proposed explanation for possible benefit from prolonged (3–6months) GnRH analogue suppression before IVF is reduced endometriosis-related inflammation affecting oocytes and endometrial receptivity. A Cochrane review of 8 RCTs involving 640 participants with endometriosis of any stage found uncertain effects of long-term GnRH treatment (minimum 3months), compared with no pretreatment before IVF or ICSI, on clinical pregnancy, miscarriage and live birth. Prolonged GnRH agonist treatment may excessively suppress the pituitary gland, potentially impairing ovarian response and luteal function. The review also found uncertain effects on mean oocyte and embryo numbers; underlying studies were very low quality and highly heterogeneous. An RCT involving 400 infertile women with minimal or mild disease found no improvement in embryo quality, implantation or clinical pregnancy after 3months of GnRH agonists following surgical cauterization and before ART. Because postoperative GnRH agonists reduce recurrence and endometrioma formation, they may have a role for symptomatic women awaiting ART. A small RCT of stimulated IUI compared daily Decapeptyl 0.1mg for 2weeks before stimulation (n=41, ‘long protocol’) with a single 3.75mg dose followed 4weeks later by daily Decapeptyl 0.1mg for 2weeks before stimulation (n=39, ‘ultralong protocol’); both groups included all disease stages. Clinical pregnancy did not differ between protocols for minimal or mild disease. For moderate or severe disease, clinical pregnancy was significantly higher with the ‘ultralong’ protocol (50%, 10/20) than with the ‘long’ protocol (19% 4/21). No studies compare long-term GnRH agonists with long-term combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) or endometrioma surgery before ART. Evidence about pregnancy outcomes with long-term continuous oral contraceptive pill or other progestins is limited and low quality. Evidence for aromatase inhibitors added to GnRH agonist pretreatment is likewise limited and low quality; a retrospective cohort of 126 women with endometriomas reported better IVF outcomes with daily Letrozole alongside GnRH agonists. Studies have shown Elagolix, an oral second generation GnRH receptor antagonist, to improve endometriosis-related dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and non-menstrual pelvic pain. Its immediate pituitary gonadotrophin suppression is described as avoiding the initial GnRH agonist flare and providing an immediate effect. A double-blind randomised trial of Elagolix 200mg twice daily versus placebo for two weeks before IVF in patients with endometriosis was underway.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Evidence is insufficient to recommend GnRH agonists or hormonal contraceptives before ART to improve live birth: Good practice point. After endometriosis surgery, suppressive hormonal treatment may be considered to limit symptoms and recurrence while awaiting ART: Good practice point. Evidence is insufficient to recommend aromatase inhibitors as ART pretreatment: Good practice point. Evidence did not then support GnRH antagonists as ART pretreatment; ongoing studies were expected to inform this question: Research recommendation.

document_sections.heading: Surgery as an adjuvant/pre-treatment to ART
document_sections.content: A single retrospective cohort compared complete disease excision (n= 399) with diagnostic laparoscopy alone (n=262) before IVF/ICSI for minimal or mild endometriosis. The excision group had higher implantation, pregnancy, live birth and cumulative pregnancy rates and a shorter interval to first pregnancy; better-designed studies are needed before recommending surgery in this setting. A meta-analysis of four studies of infertile women with deep infiltrating endometriosis reported live birth rates 2.2 times (95% CI 1.42–3.46) higher after surgery before IVF than without surgery. Its authors examined complete versus incomplete surgery, bowel involvement, and surgical and IVF complications. Adding incomplete-surgery groups also favoured surgery before IVF for pregnancy per patient (odds ratio [OR] 1.63; 95% CI, 1.16–2.28). No RCTs were included, leaving a high risk of selection and allocation bias. Complication data were sparse and heterogeneous. Deep infiltrating disease often coexists with endometrioma; one included study had significantly more ovarian endometriomas in its nonsurgical IVF group, potentially biasing results. Evidence concerning endometrioma surgery before IVF is discussed under ‘Effects of endometrioma on ART’.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Further research must establish whether routine surgery before IVF benefits patients with minimal or mild disease before it can be recommended: Good practice point. Surgery before IVF solely to improve IVF outcomes in severe disease also requires further research before recommendation, given its extent and complication risks, particularly with bowel involvement; decisions should be individualized with minimal access surgeons in a multidisciplinary team: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: Complementary therapies, lifestyle measures and supplements
document_sections.content: Although acupuncture, yoga, electrotherapy and exercise have evidence of benefit for endometriosis-associated pain, evidence does not support their benefit for endometriosis-associated infertility. Oxidative stress has been implicated in this infertility, but the authors knew of no well-conducted studies establishing that antioxidants help. Evidence does not support a benefit from Chinese medicine for endometriosis-associated infertility.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Research is needed before the effectiveness of complementary therapies or lifestyle interventions for endometriosis-associated infertility can be assessed, whether used alone or alongside ART: Research recommendation.

document_sections.heading: Effects of endometriosis on intrauterine insemination
document_sections.content: Studies of intrauterine insemination with or without controlled ovarian stimulation in endometriosis are limited, especially studies reporting effects by disease stage. One RCT offers some support for gonadotropin-stimulated IUI in infertile patients with minimal or mild disease, patent tubes and partner sperm: live birth was 5.6-times higher among 53 treated patients than among 50 managed expectantly, although the confidence interval was wide (95% CI 1.18–17.4). Low-quality nonrandomised evidence suggests gonadotropin-stimulated IUI improves pregnancy rates over IUI alone (95% CI 1.1–22.5). If undertaken within 6months after surgery for minimal or mild disease, its effectiveness appeared comparable to IUI for unexplained infertility. Evidence for advanced disease is low quality. In a retrospective study of 65 patients with surgically confirmed moderate or severe disease, stimulated IUI significantly improved cumulative ongoing pregnancy compared with unstimulated IUI for the first three cycles followed by stimulation after failure (40% vs 15.6%). Another study found significantly higher pregnancy rates with IVF (111 patient, 139 cycles) or IVF after unsuccessful stimulated IUI (56 patients, 68 cycles) than with stimulated IUI alone (202 patients, 648 cycles): 47% vs 44% vs 11%. IVF's advantage over stimulated IUI was especially marked in severe disease and women >38 years of age. No studies directly compare clomiphene citrate or letrozole against gonadotropins for stimulation with IUI in endometriosis.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: For infertility with minimal or mild endometriosis, confirmed tubal patency and normal seminal fluid parameters, gonadotropin-stimulated IUI may be offered, particularly after surgery for minimal or mild disease: Weak recommendation. IUI effectiveness remains uncertain in moderate or severe disease with patent tubes; where other risks such as advancing maternal age coexist, IVF appears to yield better pregnancy rates: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: Effects of endometrioma on ovarian stimulation
document_sections.content: During stimulated IVF/ICSI, an ovary containing an endometrioma yields fewer follicles and oocytes than the healthy opposite ovary. Compared with simple cysts measuring 10–35mm, endometriomas measuring 10–50mm were associated with higher gonadotropin requirements and significantly fewer retrieved oocytes, without impaired oocyte maturation. In a comparison of cycles with endometrioma (n= 80 cycles), endometriosis without endometriotic cysts (n= 248 cycles) and tubal disease without endometriosis (n =283 cycles), endometriosis was associated with fewer retrieved oocytes regardless of cyst volume; embryo quality and pregnancy rates did not differ. A meta-analysis of 8 studies found significantly fewer mature oocytes with endometrioma but similar gonadotropin dose and duration, total and high-quality embryos, clinical pregnancy and live birth. Evidence does not establish a precise size at which endometriomas impair stimulation response. A prospective study of 64 women with unilateral lesions, size range 15– 44 mm and mean 21.8 mm, found fewer follicles and oocytes with endometriomas of 30mm or more; only 12 women had an endometrioma >30mm, and pregnancy rates did not differ. A retrospective study of 26 women with unilateral endometriomas of 5cm or more found reduced response compared with the opposite healthy ovary. Neither study established a definitive size threshold. A retrospective comparison of lesions measuring 20–29mm (n= 23), 30–39mm (n= 23) and 40–49mm (n= 21) found significantly fewer recruited follicles in the 40–49mm group; its authors proposed 4cm in diameter as a threshold for interference with ovarian response. Retrieved oocyte numbers and pregnancy rates did not differ. Size-related ART studies are small and generally poor quality, so the relevant threshold remains unsettled.

document_sections.heading: Effects of endometrioma surgery on ART outcomes
document_sections.content: Two systematic reviews and meta-analyses assessed surgery before ART. One found that ovarian cystectomy did not improve live birth (5 studies, 655 women) or pregnancy rates (11 studies, 1,512 women) relative to no surgery. Another review of 10 studies found no significant improvement in pregnancy or live birth over expectant management and no differences in retrieved oocytes, embryos created or gonadotropin dose. A retrospective comparison involved 26 women undergoing 44 ART cycles with an endometrioma in place and 53 women undergoing 58 cycles after laparoscopic resection. Cancellation for poor ovarian response and/or failed retrieval was significantly more frequent after cystectomy (13.7% versus 0%); live birth did not differ significantly (23.7% versus 26.1% with surgery). Few studies compare surgical approaches. A review found more oocytes retrieved after sclerotherapy than after laparoscopic cystectomy, with similar clinical pregnancy. A prospective cross-sectional study compared laparoscopic cystectomy (n =57) with ethanol sclerotherapy at retrieval (n =44). Live birth and cumulative pregnancy did not differ significantly, but endometrioma recurrence was higher after sclerotherapy (p=.017).

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Do not routinely operate on ovarian endometriomas before ART: current evidence indicates neither a negative effect of the endometrioma on live birth nor a positive effect of its removal on live birth, while surgery is likely to reduce ovarian reserve: Strong recommendation. Excision or ablation before ART may be considered to control endometriosis-related symptoms or improve access to follicles at retrieval; evidence does not establish a lesion-size threshold for surgery: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: GnRH agonist versus GnRH antagonist protocols
document_sections.content: An RCT covering 246 ICSI cycles in minimal or mild endometriosis and endometrioma, with or without prior resection, found similar implantation and clinical pregnancy after GnRH agonist and GnRH antagonist stimulation protocols. A retrospective analysis of 1,180 IVF cycles across all endometriosis stages likewise found no clinical-pregnancy difference between these downregulation approaches. A retrospective cohort of 386 women showed a tendency toward higher live birth with GnRH agonists in minimal or mild disease (42.8% vs 26.7%), but no difference in moderate or severe disease. Among 342 women with reduced ovarian reserve after endometrioma cystectomy, a retrospective study found no implantation or clinical-pregnancy difference, although prolonged GnRH agonist protocols tended toward better clinical outcomes. In a retrospective analysis of 284 IVF cycles, long GnRH protocols yielded higher clinical pregnancy (25% vs 12%) and live birth (18% vs 8%) per fresh, but not frozen, embryo transfer than antagonist protocols; cumulative live birth per cycle did not differ.

document_sections.heading: GnRH agonist protocols
document_sections.content: A meta-analysis of 7 RCTs in infertile patients with moderate or severe disease found higher clinical pregnancy with longer rather than shorter GnRH agonist downregulation (CI 1.37–3.04). Its studies were highly heterogeneous, and three RCTs were low quality. A duration subgroup analysis of 14 non-RCT studies found no significant clinical-outcome differences among ‘short’, ‘long’, and ‘ultralong’ protocols; its authors advised against disregarding non-RCT findings. A later meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (943 participants) indicated that an ultra-long GnRH agonist protocol with 3months of downregulation could improve clinical pregnancy over a long protocol (CI 1.11–1.55). Effectiveness did not differ by disease stage, and OHSS did not increase. This review included RCTs only, had low overall heterogeneity, added two studies to the earlier meta-analysis and excluded one study from subgroup analysis because of inappropriate grouping; it was described as offering good-quality evidence.

document_sections.heading: Progestogens
document_sections.content: Oral progestogens have been proposed instead of GnRH analogues to prevent a premature LH surge during controlled ovarian stimulation, with oral dosing and lower cost as possible advantages. They make the endometrium unreceptive, requiring all embryos to be frozen for later transfer. No RCT directly compares oral progestogens with GnRH analogues for pituitary suppression during ART stimulation in endometriosis. A retrospective case-controlled study of 244 women with advanced disease undergoing IVF/ICSI and FET found no differences in oocyte, embryo, implantation, clinical pregnancy or ongoing pregnancy outcomes between medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), dosed at 4 or 10 mg/day from menstrual cycle day 3, and GnRH agonist protocols. An RCT in 450 women with severe disease compared oral progestogens alongside human menopausal gonadotropin (hMG): retrieved oocytes were marginally higher with MPA than with dydrogesterone or progesterone (9.3±5.7 vs. 8.0±4.5 vs. 7.8±5.2), without significant differences in fertilisation or pregnancy. The authors knew of no assessments of progestogen pituitary suppression during ART in stages other than severe disease.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Either GnRH agonist or GnRH antagonist downregulation may be offered for IVF in endometriosis because clinical pregnancy and live birth differences have not been demonstrated: Strong recommendation. Data do not sufficiently favour either protocol at particular disease stages: Strong recommendation. If using a GnRH agonist, a longer protocol may be considered, especially after surgery for symptomatic disease, while exercising caution with reduced ovarian reserve: Good practice point. Evidence is insufficient to recommend oral progestogens for pituitary suppression during controlled ovarian stimulation: Weak recommendation.

document_sections.heading: Ovarian stimulation protocols Gonadotropins
document_sections.content: For ART generally, recombinant FSH, urinary FSH (purified and highly purified) and human menopausal gonadotropin have not shown overall superiority over one another. No study directly compares gonadotropin preparations or dose effects specifically during stimulation in endometriosis. Ovarian response may be reduced. A case-control study comparing ovarian endometriosis (n= 40) with tubal infertility (n =80) found poorer response and significantly greater urinary FSH requirements for adequate IVF/ICSI stimulation in the endometriosis group; the difference increased in successive cycles. Cumulative pregnancy (63.3% vs 62.6% by fifth cycle) and live birth (46.8% vs 50.9% by fifth cycle) were nevertheless similar. A retrospective comparison of 612 IVF cycles in minimal or mild endometriosis and 7,338 cycles in tubal infertility did not find reduced response; fertilisation and pregnancy rates were comparable regardless of stimulation type.

document_sections.heading: Letrozole
document_sections.content: The aromatase p450 enzyme is abnormally expressed in uterine endometrium and ectopic implants, and high endometrial expression is associated with poorer IVF outcomes. Combining an aromatase inhibitor with gonadotropins during stimulation might improve endometrial receptivity and FSH-related follicular response while reducing gonadotropin requirements. A retrospective study of 47 women with endometriosis who were negative for endometrial integrins reported higher clinical pregnancy and delivery with added letrozole than without it: 11/18 (61%) vs 4/29 (14%), and 9/18 (50%) vs 2/29 (7%), respectively. A cohort of 64 women found similar oocyte and embryo yields with or without added letrozole but did not examine pregnancy. Evidence is insufficient to recommend letrozole cotreatment with gonadotropins.

document_sections.heading: Clomiphene citrate
document_sections.content: No RCT has evaluated whether adding clomiphene citrate to gonadotropins benefits ovarian stimulation in patients with endometriosis.

document_sections.heading: Natural and modified natural cycles
document_sections.content: No study compares conventional IVF against natural-cycle IVF in endometriosis. A prospective cohort compared hCG-triggered modified natural cycles in minimal peritoneal endometriosis (n=30) with other infertility causes (n= 57). Fertilisation and clinical pregnancy per embryo transfer in the minimal-endometriosis group (80% and 23.5%, respectively) were similar to the tubal-infertility group (68.6% and 16%) but higher than in unexplained infertility (62.2% and 8.7).

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: No gonadotropin type is preferred for stimulation in endometriosis; choice depends on clinician and patient preferences: Good practice point. Stage III-IV disease may require a higher gonadotropin dose: Strong recommendation. Data are insufficient to recommend letrozole alongside gonadotrophins for stimulation: Good practice point. Evidence does not support adding clomiphene citrate to gonadotropins for stimulation: Good practice point. Evidence is unavailable to recommend natural cycles, modified natural cycles or mild stimulation during ART in endometriosis: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: Prophylactic antibiotics at the time of oocyte retrieval
document_sections.content: An endometrioma at oocyte retrieval raises concern about pelvic infection or abscess. Case reports and retrospective follow-up studies describe severe pelvic sepsis after transvaginal retrieval. No studies assess antibiotic type, dose or duration, vaginal lavage protocols, or intentional endometrioma aspiration at retrieval. Pelvic inflammatory disease after transvaginal retrieval appears uncommon: across 6years and 5,958 ultrasound-guided procedures in a retrospective study, its rate was 0.12%; only one patient out of ten with this complication had an endometrioma measuring 3–4cm. Published cases include late-presenting pelvic abscess. One report described three patients with endometriomas developing abscesses three weeks after retrieval: an intentionally aspirated endometrioma was followed by an abscess managed with antibiotics, whereas the two cases without puncture required surgery for abscess complications. Another patient required surgery for a ruptured ovarian abscess two weeks after aspiration at retrieval. Prophylactic antibiotics had been given in all reported endometrioma-associated pelvic infection cases. Reports of late abscess describe a single pre-retrieval dose of broad-spectrum antibiotics. In a retrospective follow-up of 214 IVF cycles involving persistent endometriomas (n =119), ceftriaxone was given intramuscularly at 1g for four days, starting two hours before retrieval. No endometrioma was intentionally aspirated; six (3%) were punctured accidentally, and no pelvic abscess was reported, corresponding to a very low estimated risk (0.0, CI 0.0–1.7%). That study used povidone-iodine vaginal disinfection followed by sterile isotonic saline; other reports mentioned lavage without specifying technique. A retrospective cohort covering 4years examined acute infection in endometriosis irrespective of ART. Of 10 admitted patients, only 3 had undergone oocyte retrieval and had an endometrioma. Its authors suggested that some suspected ART–endometrioma complications might instead be sporadic endometriosis-related events.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Evidence is insufficient for routine prophylactic antibiotics during transvaginal retrieval in endometriosis, although antibiotics should be considered with an endometrioma: Good practice point. No evidence favours a particular vaginal lavage method before retrieval: Good practice point. Do not electively aspirate an endometrioma during retrieval unless needed to reach follicles; if it is punctured, consider an extended antibiotic course: Good practice point. Counsel women with endometriosis to report symptoms suggesting infection after transvaginal retrieval: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: Method of fertilisation in couples with endometriosis and normal sperm parameters
document_sections.content: Evidence linking endometriosis to impaired fertilisation is conflicting. Several studies found lower fertilisation, particularly with moderate or severe rather than minimal or mild disease. Proposed explanations include impaired oocyte quality and altered peritoneal fluid interfering with sperm binding to the zona-pellucida. One RCT in couples with endometriosis and normozoospermic semen randomly assigned 786 sibling oocytes to conventional IVF or ICSI. ICSI yielded significantly higher fertilisation (73.3±23% vs 54.7±31.9%), more mean day 2 embryos (5.2±3.4% vs 3.6±2.9%) and more cryopreserved embryos (3±3.5% versus 1.5±1.6%), but not more cryopreserved blastocysts. Triploid fertilisation was significantly higher after IVF (3.9±8.7% vs 0.9±3.1%). Implantation, clinical and ongoing pregnancy, and miscarriage did not differ between IVF and ICSI in fresh or frozen cycles. A retrospective study of 368 couples without male-factor infertility found no difference in clinical pregnancy or cumulative live birth after IVF or ICSI between women with an endometrioma in place and those previously treated by laparoscopic cystectomy. No study directly compares IVF and ICSI fertilisation and pregnancy outcomes in endometriosis against other infertility causes. Indirect evidence reports equivalent IVF and ICSI fertilisation for tubal infertility but higher fertilisation with ICSI for PCOS, potentially suggesting an oocyte contribution resembling that proposed in endometriosis. A retrospective study of 503 IVF cycles found similar fertilisation in endometriosis and other infertility causes (64.1%±25.5 vs 63.9%±24.8).

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: For endometriosis without male-factor infertility, evidence is insufficient to recommend ICSI instead of standard IVF: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: Frozen embryo transfer cycles
document_sections.content: Impaired endometrial receptivity has been proposed as a contributor to endometriosis-associated infertility. However, a retrospective cohort comprising 459 euploid frozen embryo transfer (FET) cycles in 328 patients found no differences in clinical pregnancy, pregnancy loss or live birth between patients with and without endometriosis, suggesting no endometrial effect in that comparison.

document_sections.heading: Natural, modified and artificial frozen embryo transfers
document_sections.content: No studies directly compare natural or modified natural with artificial-cycle regimens specifically in endometriosis. A comparison of natural-cycle preparation for frozen-thawed transfer found similar implantation, clinical pregnancy, live birth and miscarriage in moderate or severe endometriosis (n= 233 cycles) and tubal infertility (n= 300 cycles). A small retrospective study suggested better clinical pregnancy after intrauterine hCG injection a day before frozen transfer in an artificial cycle (n =46 vs n= 135 controls). A larger cohort found significantly higher clinical pregnancy with hCG in artificial frozen transfers for endometriosis-associated infertility (57.7% n= 355 vs 49% n= 296, p= 0.027), but not higher live birth (45.6% vs 38.5%).

document_sections.heading: Downregulation protocols for frozen embryo transfers.
document_sections.content: A retrospective cohort of artificial frozen-transfer cycles across infertility types (n =1,003 cycles), including endometriosis, suggested higher live birth with GnRH agonist cotreatment than without it. In another study of patients with endometriosis, hormone replacement plus GnRH agonist (n =303 cycles) produced significantly higher clinical pregnancy (55.6% vs 43.2%) and live birth (43.5% vs 33.5%) than hormone replacement alone (n =2,936 cycles). No study compares GnRH agonist and GnRH antagonist protocols for artificial frozen transfer in endometriosis.

document_sections.heading: Letrozole
document_sections.content: The authors identified only low-quality evidence suggesting that letrozole during a frozen embryo transfer cycle improves clinical pregnancy in patients with endometriosis (n =17), compared with a group without endometriosis or letrozole (n=105).

document_sections.heading: Atosiban
document_sections.content: In an RCT, Atosiban, described as an oxytocin antagonist, was given 30minutes before frozen embryo transfer. Compared with controls, clinical pregnancy was significantly higher (58.3% vs 38.3% n=60 each arm), as was implantation (41% vs 23.4%). Live birth was not assessed.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Evidence is insufficient to recommend natural-cycle over medicated-cycle frozen-thawed embryo transfer, or the reverse, in endometriosis: Good practice point. Evidence is insufficient to support letrozole or atosiban during frozen-transfer cycles in endometriosis: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: Elective freeze all embryos
document_sections.content: Because endometriosis depends on sex steroids, IVF-associated hyperstimulation might worsen disease or endometrial receptivity and impair implantation; elective ‘freeze all’ with deferred transfer, or segmental IVF, has therefore been proposed. Three retrospective studies examined this approach. A matched cohort of 135 patients found higher cumulative ongoing pregnancy with deferred than fresh transfer (34.8% vs 17.8%, p=0.0005), without a live-birth difference. A study in mild disease (n=521 IVF/ICSI cycles) reported higher live birth in the first frozen transfer after a freeze-all cycle (33.7% vs 28.4%). In advanced moderate or severe disease, freeze-all (n= 506) was associated with significantly higher implantation (34.4% vs 25.5%, OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.26–2.02), clinical pregnancy (51.8% vs 38.8%, OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.25–2.3) and live birth (45.3% vs 31.8%, OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.27–2.39) than fresh transfer (n =255). Its subgroup analysis suggested greater clinical-pregnancy and live-birth benefit when more than 15 oocytes were recruited; gestation age and birth weight did not differ. A meta-analysis of six studies of moderate methodological quality, involving 3,010 patients, found more frequent live birth after frozen than fresh transfer (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.13–2.08, p= 0.007). The authors knew of no RCT comparing elective ‘freeze all’ or segmented IVF directly with conventional IVF specifically for endometriosis.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: There is no evidence that Freeze all is better than fresh embryo transfer for patients with endometriosis: Good practice point.

document_sections.heading: Luteal phase support
document_sections.content: Endometrial biopsies and progesterone measurements have demonstrated a luteal-phase defect in women with endometriosis. Proposed contributors to corpus luteum dysfunction include pituitary–ovarian abnormalities, reduced steroid production, luteal-cell dysfunction and hyperprolactinemia; causation remains uncertain and probably multifactorial. A low-quality IVF study compared luteal support with vaginal progesterone inserts 100mg twice or daily (n=94), inserts thrice daily (n =75), and 8% progesterone vaginal gel once daily (n =100). Ongoing and biochemical pregnancy rates did not differ significantly among groups.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: When providing luteal-phase support during IVF, do not distinguish between patients with and without endometriosis: Good practice point.
